items.text: Paid media and analytics tend to show salary movement faster early on; SEO and content specialists typically catch up by year 4-5 with a real portfolio.
Somewhere between rung one and rung two, most people in digital marketing pick a lane, whether they decide it deliberately or drift into it by default.
Being able to touch every channel a little is useful at rung one.
A title jump from a small company that never actually gave you ownership of a budget or a person does not transfer well when you interview at a company that takes the manager title literally.
Every fork above eventually needs you to defend a number to a non-marketing stakeholder.

visuals.heading: Proof That Actually Moves You Up

blocks.heading: Proof That Actually Moves You Up

items.text: The right skill mix for your fork: Google Analytics/GA4 and a data tool (Excel, Looker Studio) for every fork, plus channel-specific tools: Google Ads and Meta Ads Manager for paid media, Ahrefs or Semrush for SEO, an email/CRM platform (HubSpot, Mailchimp) for content and lifecycle work.

Proof of work over certificates: a ranked page you took from zero, a campaign with a documented before/after number, or a content piece tied to a measurable lead is worth more in an interview than any certificate alone.

Communication: the ability to explain why a campaign worked or failed in plain language to a non-marketing stakeholder becomes as important as the technical skill itself once you approach manager level.

Market positioning of yourself: a specialist known for one specific, defensible outcome ("I grew organic leads 40% in nine months") gets hired and promoted faster than a generalist with a long, unfocused skills list.

Personal fit: match the fork to your actual temperament (see the table above), because forcing yourself into a fast-feedback fork like paid media when you are naturally research-driven usually shows up as burnout, not growth.

Financial reality: free and low-cost routes (Google Skillshop, HubSpot Academy, Meta Blueprint) cover the fundamentals for every fork; a paid certification or bootcamp is worth it only when it adds mentorship, a real project with feedback, or placement access you cannot get for free, not for the certificate itself.
